en: The Nirālambopaniṣad: I worship Hari, who is without support— that which is the object of support for the knower, the known, and perfect knowledge, wherein the state of object and subject never exists at any time.
Oṃ. That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, only the full remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the Guru, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss;
who is beyond the phenomenal world, peaceful, without support, and pure radiance.
He who, having relied upon the supportless, abandons that which has a support—he is both a renunciant and a yogi, and he attains the state of absolute liberation. ||1||
For the sake of pacifying all misfortunes of these ignorant beings,
I shall now speak, having raised whatever doubts there may be regarding everything that ought to be understood.

What is Brahman? Who is Īśvara? Who is the individual soul (jīva)? What is primordial nature (prakṛti)? Who is the Supreme Self (paramātman)? Who is Brahmā? Who is Viṣṇu? Who is Rudra? Who is Indra? Who is Śamana? He is Śamana. Who is Sūrya? Who is Candra? Who are the gods (surāḥ)? Who are the asuras? Who are the piśācas? Who are human beings? Who are women? Who are animals and so forth? What is the immobile world? Who are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth? What is caste (jāti)? What is action (karma)? What is inaction (akarma)? What is knowledge (jñāna)? What is ignorance (ajñāna)?

"What is happiness? What is suffering? What is heaven? What is hell? What is bondage? What is liberation? Who is the one to be worshipped? Who is the disciple? Who is the wise man? Who is the fool? What is demonic? What is austerity? What is the supreme state? What is to be grasped? What is not to be grasped? Who is the renunciant?"—anticipating these questions, he says: "Brahman. (3)

He said: "That which appears as the Great One (Mahat), ego (Ahaṅkāra), earth, water, fire, air, and space; which is vast in form through the cosmic egg (aṇḍakośa); which consists of the nature of action, knowledge, and objects; which is non-dual, free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), augmented by all powers, beginningless and endless, pure, auspicious, peaceful, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)—that Consciousness (caitanya) which is thus designated by such terms as 'Brahman' and 'Īśvara' is indeed the Lord.

Brahman itself, having resorted to its own power called Prakṛti, created the worlds and entered them as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin); because it governs the intellect, senses, and so forth of Brahmā and the others, it is the Īśvara. || 4 ||

And as for the term "jīva" (individual soul), it refers to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Indra, and the others by way of their names and forms; through the power of false superimposition, such as "I am gross," one becomes a jīva. Although I am one, I appear as many jīvas due to the distinctions among the constituent elements that initiate the body. || 5 ||

And as for "primordial nature" (prakṛti), it is indeed the power of Brahman itself, consisting of the intellect whose capacity is the creation of the manifold and variegated world from the presence of Brahman. || 6 ||
And because it is superior to the body and so forth, Brahman alone is the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 7 ||

He is Brahmā, He is Viṣṇu, He is Indra, He is Śamana, He is Sūrya, and He is Candra; they are the Asuras, they are the Piśācas, they are human beings, they are women, they are the animals and so forth, they are the stationary objects, and they are the Brāhmaṇas and the rest. || 8 ||
All this, indeed, is Brahman; there is no diversity whatsoever here. || 9 ||
And as for "birth": there is no birth of skin, nor of blood, nor of flesh, nor of bone;
there is no birth of the self—birth is merely a conceptual construction of conventional usage. (10)

"Action" (*karman*) refers to that very action performed with the conviction "I am doing these deeds" through the senses, being rooted in the internal self (*adhyātma*). "Inaction" (*akarma*) refers to that which, due to the egoism of being the agent and enjoyer, is of the nature of bondage and the cause of birth and so forth; specifically, it is the attachment to results in obligatory and occasional sacrifices, vows, austerities, gifts, and the like. (11–12)

And "knowledge" (jñāna) is the direct experiential realization—attained through the restraint of the body and senses, the service of a true guru, and the processes of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption—that the nature of the seer and the seen is that which abides within all, is equal toward all, and like objects such as a pot or cloth, is changeless; for among all modifications, there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from consciousness. || 13 ||

And ignorance is the knowledge falsely imagined through the distinctions of various selves—such as gods, animals, humans, and immobile beings; women and men; castes and stages of life; and the conditions of bondage and liberation—within the non-dual Brahman, which is the all-pervading essence of everything, just like the delusion of a snake in a rope. 14.
And having known that which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss as "happiness," that very state which is of the form of bliss is itself happiness. || 15 ||
"Suffering" means that the very conceptualization of sense objects, which is of a non-self nature, is itself suffering. || 16 ||
And "heaven" is association with the virtuous;
"hell" is indeed association with people who are objects of the worldly cycle of existence and are devoid of virtue. (17)
And as for "bondage" (bandha): bondage is the mental construct (saṅkalpa) such as "I am born," which arises from the beginningless latent impressions of ignorance (avidyā-vāsanā). || 18 ||
The conceptualization of the veil of saṃsāra—the sense of "mine-ness" regarding father, mother, siblings, wife, children, house, garden, and field—is bondage. || 19 ||
Bondage is the volitional ideation of the ego-sense, such as the sense of being an agent and so forth. || 20 ||
The bondage of one whose resolve is fixed on the attainment of the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), is [the eighth]. || 21 ||
The mental construction of desire for worshiping gods, humans, and so forth, is bondage. || 22 ||
The mental resolve regarding the eightfold yoga of Yama and the rest is bondage. || 23 ||
The conceptualization of the duties and actions pertaining to the castes and stages of life is bondage. || 24 ||
Bondage consists of the mental constructs of command, fear, doubt, and the qualities of the self. || 25 ||
The conceptualization of knowledge regarding the rules and procedures for sacrifice, vows, austerity, and charity is bondage. (26)
The volitional thought that seeks only liberation is bondage. || 27 ||
Bondage arises solely from conceptual construction. || 28 ||

And as for "liberation" (mokṣa): through the investigation of eternal and non-eternal entities, liberation is the destruction of the bondage of attachment to all fields and the sense of "mine-ness" regarding the objects of pleasure and pain within the non-eternal cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 29 ||
And as for the term "to be worshipped," the Guru is the one to be worshipped, for he is the one who leads [the disciple] to the Brahman that is consciousness residing within all bodies. || 30 ||
And as for the "disciple," it is Brahman alone that remains as the disciple, whose knowledge has plunged into and destroyed the phenomenal world (prapañca). || 31 ||
And "the wise one" (vidvān) refers to one who knows his own conscious nature abiding within all.
And "deluded" means one who is deluded by being mounted upon the state of egoism, such as the sense of agency and so forth. || 33 ||

And that which is called "demoniac" (āsura) is the austerity practiced by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Indra, and others out of a desire for sovereignty; it is a penance characterized by extreme passion, hatred, violence, and hypocrisy, whereby one torments the inner self through fasting, chanting, fire-sacrifices, and the like. 34.

And austerity is that which, by means of the fire of direct knowledge—that "Brahman is truth and the world is illusory"—causes the scorching of the seeds of volition that had previously been perfected through the desire for the sovereignty of Brahmā and others; this is austerity. (35)

And as for the phrase "the supreme state" (paramaṃ padam): that which is higher than the vital breaths, the senses, the internal organs, the qualities, and so forth—the eternal, liberated abode of Brahman, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—is the supreme state. || 36 ||
And that which is to be grasped is the nature of pure consciousness alone, devoid of any delimitation by space, time, or substance. || 37 ||

And "ungraspable" means that the contemplation of the reality of the world—which consists of the objects of the intellect and senses produced by *māyā* and distinct from one's own true nature—is ungraspable. || 38 ||

One who is called a *saṃnyāsī* is he who, having renounced all dharmas and become free from "mine-ness" (*nirmama*) and egoism (*nirahaṅkāra*), has approached the refuge of Brahman as his highest goal; and through the knowledge arising from the experience of the meaning of the great sayings (*mahāvākya*)—such as "That thou art," "I am Brahman," "All this is indeed Brahman," and "There is no diversity here at all"—having resolved, "I am indeed Brahman," that independent ascetic who moves about in non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is a *saṃnyāsī*, he is liberated, he is worthy of worship, he is a yogi, he is a *paramahaṃsa*, he is an *avadhūta*, and he is a true *brāhmaṇa*.

Whoever studies this Nirālambopaniṣad through the grace of the Guru becomes purified by fire, he becomes purified by air; he does not return again, he does not return again; he is not born again, he is not born again—this is the Upaniṣad. 40.
Oṃ. That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises.
When the full is taken from the full, only the full remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Nirālambopaniṣad.
